strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across all 50 Metaworld-ML1 tasks plus dense and sparse Box-Pushing, with per-task IQM learning curves in the appendix and use of the IQM aggregation metric.

Reasonable set of strong baselines (SAC, CrossQ, PPO, gSDE, GTrXL) and an ablation (Section 4.3.4) that isolates the Transformer critic from the rest of the framework by swapping it back into an SAC variant.
Full hyperparameter tables are provided for all algorithms and environments, which aids reproducibility of the reported setup.

The policy-side design choices (mean action into the covariance network, layer normalization) are individually ablated, and the paper honestly reports cases where the entropy term can be removed for better performance.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to TOP-ERL (Li et al., 2024a): the paper explicitly adopts TOP-ERL's transformer-based critic with attention over trajectory segments, N-step returns, and no importance sampling. The main delta is replacing the episodic policy with a step-based policy and feeding chunked actions into the critic; this is an incremental architectural change rather than a new method.

The central claimed contribution (gradient-level averaging of N-step targets, Contributions 2 and 3) is never ablated: there is no experiment comparing gradient-level averaging against target-level averaging, or against plain 1-step returns, so the mechanism the paper claims as its key novelty is unsupported.

Theoretical analysis is weak: the variance derivation (Eq. 2, 4, Appendix B) assumes i.i.d. rewards and gamma=1, both unrealistic; rewards within trajectories are temporally correlated, and no analysis under discounting or correlated rewards is given.

A fundamental soundness issue is unaddressed: n-step returns computed from off-policy replay data (step-based SAC with a replay buffer) are biased without importance-sampling or similar corrections. The paper claims 'no importance sampling needed' but provides no theoretical or empirical justification for why the bias is acceptable in the off-policy step-based setting.

Hyperparameter fairness is questionable: e.g., 'number samples' of 1000-2000 for SAC/CrossQ/T-SAC vs. 16000 for PPO, 'epochs 1000' for SAC, buffer of 5000 trajectories for T-SAC vs. 1e6 transitions for SAC. The differences are extreme, poorly justified, and make the headline 16%-improvement claim (Table 1) hard to attribute to the method rather than tuning.

Table 1 reports single numbers without confidence intervals, seed counts, or statistical tests; some baseline results (e.g., CrossQ at 50% overall on Metaworld, PPO at 2% on dense Box-Pushing) are surprising and presented without commentary.
No compute/wall-clock comparison despite a Transformer critic that is substantially more expensive than an MLP critic; no code release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility.

Writing quality is below bar for a top venue: e.g., 'Experiments results', 'Figure 4.2' mis-reference, 'Paragraph 3.1' vs. Section 3.1, 'presented in the Figure 2', missing punctuation in the abstract, and an apparently incorrect arXiv ID for the CrossQ citation (1902.05605).

The ablation in 4.3.1 (mean into covariance network) shows no substantial IQM benefit, undermining the framing of the policy modifications as contributions; the entropy-removal study is based on only 8 runs of a single task.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and practically important problem: improving Q-value estimation in SAC with sparse rewards and multi-phase manipulation tasks.

The idea of shifting action chunking from the actor to the critic is a reasonably interesting framing, and the trajectory-level replay buffer with a causal Transformer critic that predicts returns for all partial action sequences is a sensible engineering design.
The evaluation covers a large benchmark (50 Metaworld ML1 tasks plus dense/sparse Box-Pushing), with per-task learning curves provided in the appendix and IQM as an aggregation metric.
Ablations are included for the main design choices (covariance augmentation, layer normalization, entropy term, Transformer vs. MLP critic).
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work: the paper itself states it adopts a similar transformer-based critic design to TOP-ERL (Li et al., 2024a), only replacing the episodic policy with a step-based policy. N-step returns, averaged multi-step targets, and transformer critics are all well-established; the incremental delta over TOP-ERL is not clearly delineated.

Technical soundness concerns: (i) the variance analysis (Eqs. 2-4, Appendix B) assumes i.i.d. rewards and gamma = 1, both unrealistic in the RL settings the paper targets; correlations along trajectories are exactly why N-step returns have high variance, so the derivation's relevance is questionable. (ii) The claim that 'gradient-level averaging' of separate n-step losses preserves variance-reduction benefits while avoiding signal dilution is asserted but never formally analyzed or empirically isolated; averaging losses and averaging returns are statistically very different operations, and this central claim needs support. (iii) There is an apparent mismatch between the critic, which outputs Q-values over action sequences, and the policy objective (Eq. 8), which uses Q(s_t, a_t); how a single-action Q-value is extracted from the sequence critic is not specified.

Notation and writing issues undermine clarity: Eq. (6) sums over partial sequences but writes the target as G^(n) rather than G^(i); n vs. N are used inconsistently; 'signal dilution' arguments and the pointer to 'Paragraph 3.1' are confusing; 'Cover Page' appears on every page, and the paper reads like an early draft.

Baseline comparisons are questionable: hyperparameters in Tables 2-4 differ drastically across algorithms (e.g., SAC with 1000 epochs vs. T-SAC with 5; CrossQ 'number samples' of 1; T-SAC buffer size of 5000), and SAC/CrossQ score 0% on Box-Pushing, which strongly suggests weakly tuned baselines rather than a fair comparison. Whether hyperparameters were tuned equally per algorithm is not discussed.

Contradictions between claims and setup: the paper emphasizes the entropy-regularized SAC framework and exploration benefits, yet Tables 3-4 show the entropy coefficient is set to 0 for T-SAC on Box-Pushing, and the ablation itself shows removing the entropy term helps on assembly-v2. This muddies the method's actual identity and the interpretation of gains.

Number of seeds and statistical significance are not reported; many per-task curves in Figures 3-4 show large overlaps between T-SAC and baselines, and the headline '16% higher success rate' is an aggregate over heterogeneous tasks without per-task significance analysis.

Sparse-reward claims are weaker than advertised: on the sparse Box-Pushing task, gSDE achieves 60% vs. T-SAC's 58%, directly contradicting the narrative that the method excels in sparse-reward environments.

No code release is mentioned, and given the many nonstandard details (trajectory replay buffer, gradient-level aggregation, custom policy network with detached mean input), reproducibility is a concern.

The ablation study uses inconsistent task subsets across experiments (11 tasks vs. 5 tasks vs. all 50 tasks), making it hard to attribute the reported gains to the core contributions (transformer critic + N-step returns) versus the auxiliary policy-side design choices.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practical question in deep RL: improving critic-side temporal credit assignment, and the idea of shifting action chunking from the actor to the critic is a reasonably interesting angle.

Empirical coverage is broad: evaluation on all 50 Metaworld-ML1 tasks plus dense and sparse Box-Pushing tasks, with per-task IQM learning curves in the appendix and several ablations (covariance augmentation, layer normalization, entropy term, SAC variant with MLP critic).
The reported gains are substantial (86% overall Metaworld success vs. 70% for SAC, 92%/58% on dense/sparse Box-Pushing), and the sparse-reward/multi-phase setting is a genuinely difficult regime.
The hyperparameter tables in the appendix provide a good level of implementation detail that supports reproducibility.
The variance analysis of averaged N-step targets (Appendix B) is a useful pedagogical treatment, even if the underlying assumptions are idealized.
weaknesses: The central technical claim is questionable. The paper distinguishes 'gradient-level averaging' (Eq. 7) from averaging N-step targets and claims this preserves variance-reduction benefits while avoiding signal dilution. However, since all loss terms L_i share the same critic parameters, summing/averaging the losses is mathematically identical to optimizing the MSE against averaged targets: ∇(1/n Σ L_i) = (1/n) Σ ∇L_i by linearity of the gradient. The claimed decoupling appears to be an equivalence, not a distinction, and the paper provides no analysis or experiment demonstrating that the proposed scheme behaves differently from (or better than) simply averaging the targets. A direct ablation (gradient-level vs. target-level averaging) is missing, despite this being Contribution 2.

Novelty is limited. The critic architecture and the N-step return machinery are explicitly adopted from TOP-ERL (Li et al., 2024a); the main delta is using a step-based policy instead of an episodic policy. The additional design choices (mean fed into covariance network, layer norm) are small heuristics. The paper would benefit from a clearer delineation of what is genuinely new versus inherited.

The claimed elimination of importance sampling is asserted but not analyzed. The critic is trained on N-step returns collected under the behavior policy, and actions a_{t+1:t+n} from the replay buffer are fed as inputs—both introduce off-policy distribution mismatch. How the twin-Q trick from SAC interacts with the transformer critic (which appears to output a single Q) is not specified.

The variance analysis assumes i.i.d. rewards (Eq. 2), which is unrealistic in control tasks where rewards are strongly temporally correlated, and it ignores the correlation with the bootstrap term. The conclusions drawn from this idealized model are therefore weakly supported.

Baseline fairness and credibility are concerns. Several baseline results look suspicious (e.g., SAC scoring 0% on Box-Pushing Dense while T-SAC achieves 92%; SAC with 'number samples 8' and 'epochs 1000' in Table 3; CrossQ at 50% on Metaworld, well below published numbers). There is no discussion of how baselines were tuned, no confidence intervals or seed counts in Table 1, and no wall-clock/compute comparison despite the transformer critic being substantially more expensive than an MLP.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code release is mentioned, several notation inconsistencies (N vs. n, t ranges, 'episode within a trajectory') make the algorithm description hard to follow precisely, and references contain errors (e.g., the CrossQ citation year/arXiv ID appear wrong; the fancy_gym citation lacks a year/venue).

Ablations are narrow: ablation tasks cover only 5–11 of 50 tasks, the 'SAC variant' comparison is only shown as aggregate curves, and key alternatives (e.g., MLP critic with N-step returns at the target level, different max_length values) are not tested, so the source of the gains cannot be cleanly attributed.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: moving action/trajectory chunking from the actor to the critic, combining a causal Transformer critic over short action windows with multi-horizon N-step targets without importance sampling; the positioning against TOP-ERL, Q-chunking, and CrossQ is explicit and fair

Comprehensive and largely convincing evaluation: 50 Meta-World ML1 tasks plus Box-Pushing (dense/sparse) and Gymnasium MuJoCo, IQM with bootstrap CIs, multiple seeds, and per-task curves in the appendix

Extensive ablation study (causal mask, self-attention, ResNet blocks, supervision-window lengths, number of sampled windows, policy-side chunking, GRU/LSTM critics) that supports each design choice, including a demonstration that the Transformer critic outperforms recurrent critics under identical training

Useful theoretical analysis in appendices (variance reduction from target-level and gradient-level averaging, plus reuse/coverage analysis of critic-side chunking), which explains why chunking helps sparse-reward credit assignment and why training can be target-free

Honest reporting of limitations: weaker MuJoCo results (Hopper, Walker2d), instability in sparse-reward regimes without a target network, lower seed counts for some settings, and differences in budget/aggregation protocol vs. baselines are disclosed
Strong reproducibility: detailed algorithm pseudocode, per-benchmark hyperparameter tables, environment/reward definitions, and a committed code release
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the Transformer critic design, causal masking, prefix-conditioned N-step targets, and the IS-free target are explicitly borrowed from TOP-ERL (Li et al., 2024a); the main delta is using them inside a step-based SAC, and the freezing schedule amounts to hard-copy target updates, which is a known technique

Some baseline comparisons are not fully controlled: several Meta-World baseline numbers come from prior publications/released runs rather than re-runs, budgets differ (T-SAC 5M vs. larger budgets for baselines), and sparse-reward Box-Pushing uses only 4 seeds; CrossQ uses 4 seeds on Meta-World, weakening statistical claims

Claims of 'state-of-the-art' are qualified by context: on MuJoCo, T-SAC is middling to weaker on Hopper/Walker2d and requires task-specific hyperparameters (initial std, target entropy) and action masks, suggesting sensitivity and reduced generality

The critic includes the state only at the first position (shared across prefixes), a design choice with potential aliasing effects across horizons that is not analyzed; the relationship between the empirical gradient-level averaging and the naive target averaging of Daley et al. (2024) (which they show destabilizes learning) is asserted rather than rigorously justified
Theory relies on strong equicorrelation/exchangeability assumptions; the main theoretical claims are essentially known variance-reduction results re-derived in this setting
About 2x the wall-clock cost of SAC per 1M steps; the efficiency comparison in Fig. 2 is somewhat buried and the compute-equivalence of the reported gains is not fully addressed

strengths: Broad empirical coverage: 57 tasks across Meta-World ML1, Gymnasium MuJoCo, and FANCYGYM Box-Pushing, with IQM metrics and bootstrap confidence intervals; per-task curves are provided in the appendix.
Extensive ablation suite (Transformer components, multi-horizon window, chunk length, per-step target sampling, RNN backbones) that isolates design choices on at least one environment.

The critic-side analysis in Appendices C, D, and G (variance reduction of averaged N-step returns and bootstrap-reuse/sparse-reward propagation counts) is worked out in some detail, and the method description plus hyperparameter tables are thorough enough to aid reimplementation.

Positioning relative to TOP-ERL, CrossQ, and Q-chunking is clearly articulated, and the paper is candid about limitations (e.g., reverting to target networks under sparse rewards, weaker MuJoCo results on Hopper/Walker2d).
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core idea—causal Transformer critic trained on truncated N-step targets for realized prefixes, without IS—is explicitly inherited from TOP-ERL (Li et al., 2024a); the delta is applying it to step-based SAC, which is an incremental combination rather than a conceptual advance. The 'chunking the critic' framing largely overlaps Q-chunking's action-sequence critic.

Unresolved conceptual question about the critic's semantics: Q(st, at:t+i-1) conditions on future actions, so it evaluates realized prefixes; how the actor update uses this (only the 1-step head?) and whether this biases policy gradients is never analyzed, despite being central to whether the sequence modeling actually helps the policy.

The headline 'training without a target network' claim is fragile: the freezing schedule applies only to local-motion benchmarks, and the paper concedes instability in sparse-reward regimes where the conventional target network is reinstated (App. E). This is a partial result presented as a general feature.

Baseline comparability is weak. Many baselines (BBRL, TCP, PPO, gSDE, GTrXL, TOP-ERL, SAC on Meta-World) are taken from prior publications rather than rerun; seed counts are inconsistent (8 vs 4 vs 20 vs 5); budgets differ across methods and ablations; and the success criterion (final-step-only) deviates from standard Meta-World evaluation. Aggregate claims of superiority rest on a mix of heterogeneous protocols.

Ablations are confined to Box-Pushing dense, and several ablation groups use reduced budgets (16M/10M vs the 20M default), so the evidence that the design choices generalize beyond one environment is thin.

MuJoCo results are middling to weak (worse than SAC/CrossQ on Hopper and Walker2d), which undercuts the paper's claim of a generally stronger step-based method; the benefit appears confined to specific long-horizon manipulation settings.

The variance theory relies on a restrictive equicorrelation/exchangeability model with assumed independence between rewards and bootstrap values; the bounds (e.g., 1 <= R < 4) are mostly restatements of weighted-sum algebra and provide little insight specific to this architecture, and their connection to observed stability is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Reproducibility: code is only promised 'upon acceptance', and given the many environment-specific hyperparameters (K=20 freezing, per-benchmark UTD, action masks only for some tasks), independent verification is difficult.

strengths: Broad and substantial empirical evaluation: 57 tasks across Meta-World ML1 (50 tasks), Gymnasium MuJoCo, and FancyGym Box-Pushing, with 8 seeds, IQM aggregation, and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals following rigorous reporting practice (rliable-style).

Comprehensive ablation suite (Fig. 5) covering Transformer components (causal mask, attention, residual blocks), multi-horizon supervision windows, per-step target sampling, policy-side action chunking, and backbone swaps (GRU/LSTM), which substantiates the design choices.

Honest treatment of limitations: the paper acknowledges weaker MuJoCo results (Hopper, Walker2d), sparse-reward instability requiring reinstated target updates, reduced seeds for sparse experiments, and caveats in the variance analysis.

Useful supporting analysis: variance-reduction proofs for target-level and gradient-level averaging (App. C/D), and a quantitative account of bootstrap-value reuse and sparse-reward propagation under chunked supervision (App. G), which gives intuition for why the method works.

The 'multi-step supervision, one-step policy update' framing is a clean and practical middle ground between step-based SAC and episodic/trajectory-level methods, and the comparison to a multi-step MLP critic (Q-chunking) with causal leakage analysis (Sec. 5.5.3) is a nice contribution.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core ingredients are assembled from existing work—TOP-ERL's prefix-conditioned Transformer critic with truncated N-step targets (including the no-IS trick), CrossQ's target-free motivation (here via a simple parameter-freezing schedule), and standard N-step returns. The main contribution is an adaptation/recombination for step-based SAC rather than a fundamentally new idea or method.

Baseline fairness concerns: Appendix J states that several baselines (BBRL, TCP, PPO, gSDE, GTrXL, TOP-ERL, SAC on Meta-World) use numbers from prior publications or released runs rather than being run under an identical protocol, while T-SAC is tuned by the authors with a targeted grid search. Combined with differing training budgets (5M steps for T-SAC vs. larger budgets for baselines), this weakens the headline comparisons.

Missing a key control: a plain MLP critic with multi-step N-step targets and no policy-side chunking is not clearly compared. Without it, the claimed benefit of the Transformer critic itself (vs. simply adding N-step returns to SAC) is not fully isolated; GRU/LSTM and MLP-chunking ablations are not an adequate substitute.
Off-policy bias from dropping importance sampling is acknowledged but only informally inherited from TOP-ERL; no theoretical or empirical quantification of when this bias is acceptable is provided.

Results are uneven: T-SAC is middling-to-weaker on standard MuJoCo (Ant, Hopper, Walker2d), and the target-free freezing result is restricted to locomotion with occasional instability in sparse settings, weakening the generality of the target-network-free claim.
Some experiments rest on thin evidence: sparse-reward results use 4 seeds and exhibit high variance; the hard-copy variant oscillates; per-task ablations use 4 seeds.
No code released at submission time ('upon acceptance'), which limits reproducibility verification during review.
